items.en: a win that costs so much that it is almost worthless
items.example: Winning the case was a Pyrrhic victory, as the legal fees ruined her.

items.en: an obvious problem that nobody wants to discuss
items.example: Money was the elephant in the room during the family meeting.

items.en: a question that people disagree about with no clear answer
items.example: Whether the law applies here is a moot point.

items.en: a job or gift that seems good but brings trouble
items.example: The manager's job at the struggling club proved a poisoned chalice.

items.en: a situation with no real option: take what is offered or nothing
items.example: It was Hobson's choice: pay the fee or miss the exam.

items.lemma: every cloud has a silver lining
items.en: even bad situations have some good side
items.example: I lost my job, but every cloud has a silver lining: I now run my own firm.
items.ipa: ˌevri ˈklaʊd həz ə ˌsɪlvə ˈlaɪnɪŋ

items.lemma: too many cooks spoil the broth
items.en: a job goes wrong when a large number of people try to control it
items.example: Four of us planned the party and nothing got done; too many cooks spoil the broth.
items.ipa: ˌtuː ˌmeni ˈkʊks ˌspɔɪl ðə ˈbrɒθ

items.lemma: the proof of the pudding is in the eating
items.en: you can only judge something by how it works in practice
items.example: The recipe sounds odd, but the proof of the pudding is in the eating.
items.ipa: ðə ˌpruːf əv ðə ˈpʊdɪŋ ɪz ɪn ði ˈiːtɪŋ

items.en: when you depend on others you cannot refuse what you are given
items.example: The sofa is ugly, but beggars can't be choosers.

items.en: something that seems harmless but hides a threat inside
items.example: The free software turned out to be a Trojan horse for spyware.

items.en: the one weak point in an otherwise strong person
items.example: Her Achilles' heel is that she cannot delegate.

items.en: a danger that hangs over you and could strike at any moment
items.example: The threat of closure hung over the staff like the sword of Damocles.

items.en: a hopeless search for something that cannot be found
items.example: The tip-off sent the police on a wild goose chase across the county.

items.en: to leave a problem alone so it does not cause trouble again
items.example: Raising the old row would only upset her; let sleeping dogs lie.

items.lemma: a stitch in time saves nine
items.en: acting early prevents bigger problems later
items.example: Fix the leak now, because a stitch in time saves nine.
items.ipa: ə ˌstɪtʃ ɪn ˌtaɪm ˌseɪvz ˈnaɪn

items.lemma: a leopard cannot change its spots
items.en: people do not change their basic nature
items.example: He promised to reform, but a leopard cannot change its spots.
items.ipa: ə ˌlepəd ˌkænɒt ˌtʃeɪndʒ ɪts ˈspɒts

items.en: an odd case shows that the general pattern normally holds
items.example: Few cats like water, but the exception proves the rule.

items.lemma: look a gift horse in the mouth
items.en: to criticise something that you were given free
items.example: It's not perfect, but don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
items.ipa: lʊk ə ˌɡɪft ˈhɔːs ɪn ðə ˈmaʊθ

items.en: a completely unexpected event
items.example: The news of her resignation came as a bolt from the blue.

items.en: the last work or performance of someone's career
items.example: The concert was the pianist's swan song after fifty years on stage.

items.lemma: the chickens come home to roost
items.en: bad past actions at last cause trouble for the person who did them
items.example: After years of neglect, the chickens have come home to roost.
items.ipa: ðə ˌtʃɪkɪnz kʌm ˌhəʊm tə ˈruːst

items.lemma: a red rag to a bull
items.en: something that makes a person very angry
items.example: Criticising his cooking is a red rag to a bull.
items.ipa: ə ˌred ˌræɡ tu ə ˈbʊl

items.en: a lot of fuss about something unimportant
items.example: The row over the biscuits was a storm in a teacup.

items.lemma: the thin end of the wedge
items.en: a small first step that leads to something worse
items.example: Banning one book may be the thin end of the wedge.
items.ipa: ðə ˌθɪn end əv ðə ˈwedʒ

items.en: to fight against enemies that are imaginary or pointless
items.example: Critics said he was tilting at windmills with his campaign.

items.en: a way of speaking that makes things sound much bigger than they are
items.example: Calling the meal a disaster was pure hyperbole.

items.en: the use of the same sound at the start of nearby words
items.example: Tongue twisters rely heavily on alliteration.

items.en: a phrase that puts two opposite words together
items.example: A deafening silence is a classic oxymoron.

items.en: a joke that uses a word with two meanings
items.example: The fish shop's name is a terrible pun.

items.en: a situation that seems impossible because it contains opposite facts
items.example: It is a paradox that the richest towns often feel the loneliest.

items.en: a phrase that compares two things using the word like or as
items.example: Saying someone is as brave as a lion is a simile.

items.en: the choice of words and the way they are said
items.example: The actor's clear diction carried to the back of the hall.

items.en: the rules for putting words in order in sentences
items.example: Learners often find German syntax harder than its vocabulary.

items.en: (disapproving) a dull comment that has been made too often
items.example: The speech was full of platitudes about hard work.

items.en: a statement so obviously correct that saying it adds nothing
items.example: It is a truism that money cannot buy happiness.

items.en: a hint about something rude or unpleasant
items.example: The comedian's act was full of cheap innuendo.

items.en: the rise and fall of the voice when someone speaks
items.example: She spoke with the gentle cadence of the Welsh valleys.

items.en: to make a story more interesting by adding untrue details
items.example: Grandpa loved to embellish his tales of the war at sea.

items.en: to explain a point for much too long
items.example: I won't belabour the point because you all know the facts.

items.en: to give your opinion in a boring way as if it were the only right one
items.example: He pontificated about wine for most of the dinner.

items.en: (formal) to explain an idea in great detail
items.example: The professor expounded on his theory for an hour.

items.en: (disapproving) to keep talking about the same subject in a boring way
items.example: He kept harping on about his exam results all evening.

items.en: (formal) to avoid giving a direct answer
items.example: Asked about the cost, the minister prevaricated.

items.en: to express something in a particular way
items.example: He couched his criticism in very polite language.

items.en: (disapproving) using more words than are needed
items.example: The report is verbose and could be half as long.

items.en: short and clear
items.example: Please keep your summary succinct and to the point.

items.en: short and full of meaning
items.example: He is known for his pithy remarks on city life.

items.en: using few words in a rude or unfriendly way
items.example: Her terse reply showed she did not want to talk.

items.en: using very few words in a calm way
items.example: Owen gave his usual laconic answer: fine.

items.en: (disapproving) full of fancy words
items.example: I prefer plain prose to flowery language.

items.en: comfort that you feel when you are sad or disappointed
items.example: She found solace in music after her father died.

items.en: (literary) a pleasant state of dreaming while you are awake
items.example: Tom was lost in reverie until the train jerked to a halt.

items.en: (literary) strong and passionate enthusiasm
items.example: He pursued his studies with youthful ardour.

items.en: a sad poem or song about someone who has died
items.example: The poet wrote an elegy for her brother.

items.en: (literary) a sign that something important is coming
items.example: The early snow was a harbinger of a long hard winter.

items.en: (literary) remembered as calm and happy
items.example: She often talks about the halcyon days of her childhood.

items.en: a thick dark cloud that covers a place or a feeling of gloom
items.example: A pall of smoke hung over the city for days.

items.en: a beautiful view of a wide area
items.example: From the ridge a vast vista of hills and lakes opened up.

items.en: (literary) a short stay in a place away from home
items.example: Her sojourn in Lisbon lasted barely a month.

items.en: (literary) to think about something slowly and quietly
items.example: She mused on how quickly the years had passed.

items.en: (literary) to seem to invite you to come closer
items.example: The lights of the village beckoned through the falling snow.

items.en: (literary) to charm someone completely
items.example: The old town beguiled visitors with its narrow lanes and lamps.

items.en: to stay in a bad place or situation without hope of change
items.example: He languished in prison for six years before his case was heard.

items.en: to appear as a large shape that seems threatening
items.example: Dark mountains loomed out of the mist.

items.en: to say that you are very sad about something
items.example: Critics lamented the loss of the old theatre.

items.en: lasting for only a very short time
items.example: Fame can be ephemeral in the age of social media.

items.en: (literary) too great or beautiful to be described in words
items.example: She felt an ineffable joy as the sun rose over the sea.

items.en: calm and peaceful
items.example: The lake was serene in the early morning light.

items.en: slow and relaxed in a pleasant way
items.example: He waved a languid hand towards the garden.

items.en: shining brightly especially in the dark
items.example: The luminous hands of the clock glowed in the dark room.

items.en: empty and sad with no people or comfort
items.example: The moor looked desolate in the winter rain.

items.en: looking sad and alone
items.example: A forlorn figure stood waiting at the empty station.

items.en: extremely peaceful and beautiful
items.example: They spent an idyllic week in a cottage by the sea.

items.en: dark and serious or sad
items.example: The mourners wore sombre clothes and spoke in low voices.

items.en: (literary) sounding sad and weak as if asking for help
items.example: We heard the plaintive cry of a seabird above the cliffs.

items.en: the main ideas and feelings of a particular period in history
items.example: The film perfectly captured the zeitgeist of the early nineties.

items.en: pleasure that you feel when something bad happens to someone else
items.example: There was a hint of schadenfreude in her smile when he failed.

items.en: an embarrassing mistake in a social situation
items.example: Arriving at the wedding in jeans was a real faux pas.

items.en: the strange feeling that you have already lived through the present moment
items.example: Walking into the café, Mei had a strong sense of déjà vu.

items.en: complete freedom to do whatever you think is best
items.example: The new manager was given carte blanche to redesign the shop.

items.en: the way things are now especially when people want to change them
items.example: Many residents want to keep the status quo in the old town.

items.en: a short street that is closed at one end
items.example: They live in a quiet cul-de-sac on the edge of town.

items.en: a meeting that you have arranged with someone at a particular place
items.example: Their rendezvous was at the station café at noon.

items.en: a strong feeling of worry about life or the future
items.example: The novel is full of adolescent angst about growing up.

items.en: a strong wish to travel to many places
items.example: Wanderlust took hold of him and he booked a one-way ticket.

items.en: a person who looks exactly like another person
items.example: Fatima met her doppelgänger at a conference in Leeds.

items.en: art or objects that are cheap and too sentimental
items.example: Her flat is full of seventies kitsch.

items.en: a complete and often embarrassing failure
items.example: The opening night was a total fiasco.

items.en: a person who knows a lot about a subject and loves it
items.example: Jazz aficionados travel from all over Europe to the festival.

items.en: a different side of your character that people do not usually see
items.example: On stage the shy singer turns into her bold alter ego.

items.en: the greatest work of an artist or writer
items.example: It took her twenty years to finish her magnum opus.

items.en: made or done for one purpose without earlier planning
items.example: The committee meets on an ad hoc basis.

items.en: existing in reality even if not officially accepted
items.example: After the merger Priya became the de facto head of the team.

items.en: real and honest and not false
items.example: Only bona fide students may use the library.

items.en: very new and unusual in art or music
items.example: The gallery is known for its avant-garde installations.

items.en: not excited by things because you have seen them many times
items.example: He was blasé about the prize and did not even go to the ceremony.

items.en: by itself and not together with other things
items.example: Money per se does not make people happy.

items.en: the other way round
items.example: Tom helps Amira with English and vice versa.

items.en: so often or for so long that it becomes boring or annoying
items.example: He repeated the same joke ad nauseam all evening.

items.en: a saying that means you should enjoy today and not wait
items.example: Her motto is carpe diem so she said yes to every invitation.

items.en: a sharp split between two opposite things or ideas
items.example: There is a false dichotomy between work and play.

items.en: a typical model of how something is understood
items.example: The discovery forced scientists to adopt a new paradigm.

items.en: a statement accepted as true without needing proof
items.example: It is an axiom of geometry that parallel lines never meet.

items.en: a basic principle of a belief system
items.example: Non-violence is a central tenet of the movement.

items.en: the belief that life has no meaning or value
items.example: The novel's bleak nihilism left some readers cold.

items.en: a practical way of dealing with things based on what works
items.example: Her pragmatism helped the two sides reach a deal.

items.en: the set of beliefs that guides a group or organisation
items.example: The school has a strong ethos of mutual respect.

items.en: a set of beliefs that people must accept without question
items.example: Owen refused to accept the dogma of his old party.

items.en: the belief that all events are fixed by earlier causes
items.example: Determinism leaves little room for free will.

items.en: the view that truth and values depend on the person or culture
items.example: Moral relativism makes it hard to condemn any custom.

items.en: an opinion based on incomplete evidence
items.example: Her claim is pure conjecture with no evidence behind it.

items.en: based on reasoning alone rather than on experience
items.example: Such a claim cannot be known a priori and must be tested.

items.en: (formal) to put forward an idea as a basis for argument
items.example: The theory posits that language is shaped by thought.

items.en: to need something else to be true first
items.example: Freedom of choice presupposes access to information.

items.en: (formal) to support a belief or cause publicly
items.example: She espoused the ideals of equality all her life.

items.en: to say that something is caused by or belongs to someone
items.example: Critics ascribe the novel's success to clever marketing.

items.en: to go beyond the limits of something
items.example: Great music transcends language and culture.

items.en: (formal) to describe or mark the exact limits of something
items.example: The treaty delineates the border in great detail.

items.en: to place two things side by side to show a contrast
items.example: The exhibition juxtaposes old photographs with modern ones.

items.en: depending on something else that may or may not happen
items.example: The offer is contingent on a satisfactory medical.

items.en: concerned with ideas about existence and reality
items.example: Kwame enjoys metaphysical questions about time and identity.

items.en: belonging to the nature of something itself
items.example: Money has no intrinsic value apart from what people accept.

items.en: saying the same thing twice in different words
items.example: Free gift is a tautological phrase.

items.en: so obviously true that no proof is needed
items.example: It is axiomatic that a doctor must respect privacy.

items.en: understood by only a small group with special knowledge
items.example: The lecture was far too esoteric for a general audience.

items.en: (informal) a fuss about something small
items.example: There was a kerfuffle at the door when the band arrived.

items.en: (informal) something that is very easy to do
items.example: After all that revision the exam was a doddle.

items.en: (informal) a situation in which everything is badly organised
items.example: The first rehearsal was a complete shambles.

items.en: (informal) money
items.example: He's got plenty of dosh but he never buys anyone a drink.

items.en: (informal) to study very hard for an exam
items.example: Mei spent the whole weekend swotting for her finals.

items.en: (informal) to stay away from work or school without permission
items.example: Liam skived off school to go to the match.

items.en: (informal) to waste time doing unimportant things
items.example: Stop faffing about and get your coat on.

items.en: (informal) to get something by clever or slightly dishonest methods
items.example: Amira managed to wangle a free ticket to the concert.

items.en: (informal) to complain in an annoying way
items.example: Stop whinging about the weather and enjoy the walk.

items.en: (informal) to repair or make something badly and in a hurry
items.example: Owen bodged the shelf together and it fell down within a week.

items.en: (informal) so surprised that you cannot speak
items.example: I was absolutely gobsmacked when she told me the price.

items.en: (informal) extremely tired
items.example: I'm knackered after that ten-hour shift.

items.en: (informal) very pleased about something
items.example: Kwame was chuffed to bits with his exam results.

items.en: (informal) very disappointed and upset
items.example: We were gutted when the match was cancelled.

items.en: (informal) a little hungry
items.example: I'm feeling a bit peckish so let's stop for a snack.

items.en: (informal) not stylish in a slightly embarrassing way
items.example: Those plastic flowers look really naff.

items.en: (informal) annoyed and a bit bored with something
items.example: Zofia was cheesed off about missing the last bus.

items.en: (informal) difficult to do because it needs small careful movements
items.example: Replacing the tiny screws was a fiddly job.

items.en: (informal) not honest or safe or not working well
items.example: I wouldn't buy a car from that dodgy dealer.

items.en: (informal) having no money
items.example: I can't come out tonight because I'm skint until Friday.

items.en: (informal) stupid and not showing much thought
items.example: Don't stand there looking gormless and give me a hand.

items.en: (informal) slightly annoyed
items.example: Priya was a bit miffed that nobody had called her.

items.en: (informal) ordinary and not special in any way
items.example: It's just a bog-standard laptop with nothing fancy about it.

items.en: (informal) bad-tempered and difficult to deal with
items.example: My brother gets stroppy whenever he's tired.

items.en: (informal) dirty and unpleasant
items.example: We stayed in a grotty hotel near the station.

items.en: the responsibility to prove something or to do a duty
items.example: The onus is on the landlord to prove the damage was deliberate.

items.en: protection against having to pay for loss or damage
items.example: The contract includes an indemnity against any legal costs.

items.en: the official power to make legal decisions in an area
items.example: The case falls outside the jurisdiction of this court.

items.en: a condition that must be accepted before an agreement is made
items.example: She accepted the loan with the proviso that it be repaid within a year.

items.en: a formal promise that is binding in law
items.example: The deeds contain a covenant forbidding any commercial use of the building.

items.en: a written statement that you swear is true and can use in court
items.example: Each witness signed an affidavit before the hearing.

items.en: the smallest number of people needed for a meeting to make decisions
items.example: The vote was delayed because there was no quorum.

items.en: an official pause in an activity until a problem is solved
items.example: The council imposed a moratorium on new building near the river.

items.en: the act of giving back something that was taken or lost
items.example: The court ordered restitution to the victims of the scheme.

items.en: the right or time of holding a job or property
items.example: Security of tenure protects tenants from sudden eviction.

items.en: the legal right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid
items.example: The bank placed a lien on the house until the loan was cleared.

items.en: an official order issued by a court
items.example: The firm was served with a writ demanding payment.

items.en: to officially cancel a law or decision
items.example: The council rescinded the ban after weeks of protest.

items.en: (formal) to officially end a law or agreement
items.example: The state abrogated the treaty without warning.

items.en: to act as judge in a dispute
items.example: An independent panel will adjudicate the dispute.

items.en: to lose something as a penalty
items.example: Anyone who withdraws late forfeits the deposit.

items.en: to leave money or property to someone in a will
items.example: She bequeathed her collection of books to the town library.

items.en: to take the place of something older
items.example: The new regulations supersede all previous guidance.

items.en: to declare officially that something is no longer valid
items.example: The court annulled the marriage after the deception came to light.

items.en: mentioned earlier in the same text or speech
items.example: The aforementioned clauses remain in force until further notice.

items.en: that cannot be taken away or given up
items.example: Freedom of speech is regarded as an inalienable right.

items.en: understood by everyone without being said
items.example: There was a tacit agreement not to mention the dispute.

items.en: by means of this statement or document
items.example: I hereby declare that the information above is true.

items.en: (formal) following or according to
items.example: Pursuant to the contract, payment is due within thirty days.

items.en: having no legal effect
items.example: The agreement was declared null and void by the court.

items.en: control or strong influence by one country over others
items.example: The empire's hegemony over the region lasted two centuries.

items.en: an organised violent fight against a government
items.example: The army struggled to defeat the insurgency in the mountains.

items.en: a series of rulers from the same family
items.example: The Tudor dynasty ruled England for 118 years.

items.en: a ruler with total power who uses it cruelly
items.example: The people finally rose up against the despot.

items.en: a country ruled by one person with unlimited power
items.example: Many historians describe the empire as an autocracy.

items.en: a government that is cruel or was not freely elected
items.example: The regime banned every newspaper that criticised the army.

items.en: cruel and unfair treatment of people by those in power
items.example: Many fled the country to escape political oppression.

items.en: a sudden fight by many people against those in power
items.example: The uprising was crushed within a few weeks.

items.en: an agreement to stop fighting in a war
items.example: The armistice was signed on 11 November 1918.

items.en: a serious split in an organisation especially a church
items.example: The schism divided the church for centuries.

items.en: a sudden illegal takeover of a government
items.example: The president was removed in a military coup.

items.en: a military leader who controls an area by force
items.example: Local warlords controlled the roads and demanded payment.

items.en: to take control of land that belongs to another country
items.example: The empire annexed the neighbouring province in 1878.

items.en: to give in to demands in order to avoid conflict
items.example: Attempts to appease the dictator only encouraged him.

items.en: to defeat a people and take control of them
items.example: The invaders subjugated the local population within a decade.

items.en: to take power or a position without having the right
items.example: He usurped the throne from his young nephew.

items.en: to remove a ruler from power by force
items.example: The king was deposed after a short civil war.

items.en: to surround a place with an army until it gives in
items.example: The army besieged the city for eight months.

items.en: to stop a protest or feeling by using force
items.example: Troops were sent in to quell the unrest.

items.en: using power in a cruel and unfair way
items.example: The tyrannical king taxed the peasants until they starved.

items.en: aggressive and eager to fight
items.example: The belligerent tone of the speech alarmed neighbouring states.

items.en: controlling every part of people's lives with no opposition allowed
items.example: Totalitarian states often monitor private conversations.

items.en: trying to weaken a government or an accepted system
items.example: The play was banned because the authorities found it subversive.

items.en: cruel and willing to hurt others to get what you want
items.example: The ruthless general crushed every rival.

items.en: relating to the medieval system where lords owned the land
items.example: Under the feudal system peasants worked the land for their lord.

items.en: a bad-tempered person who is often old
items.example: The old curmudgeon next door complains about everything.

items.en: (disapproving) a person who flatters powerful people to gain an advantage
items.example: The boss was surrounded by sycophants who laughed at all his jokes.

items.en: a person who dislikes and avoids other people
items.example: The novel's hero is a lonely misanthrope who lives in a lighthouse.

items.en: a person who chooses to live alone away from society
items.example: After her husband died she became a recluse.

items.en: a person who falsely claims to have skill or knowledge
items.example: The so-called healer turned out to be a charlatan.

items.en: (disapproving) a person who cares too much about small rules and details
items.example: I don't want to be a pedant but you've spelt his name wrong.

items.en: a person who knows a great deal about many subjects
items.example: Her grandfather was a polymath who spoke six languages and built clocks.

items.en: a loyal person who supports a group for many years
items.example: She is a stalwart of the local drama society.

items.en: to love someone very much and show it too much
items.example: Her grandparents dote on her.

items.en: (disapproving) to be too friendly and flattering to win favour
items.example: The waiters fawned over the famous guest.

items.en: to react angrily because you feel insulted
items.example: She bristled at the suggestion that she was too old.

items.en: very careful and paying attention to every detail
items.example: She kept meticulous records of every payment.

items.en: enjoying being with other people
items.example: Zofia is gregarious and never happier than at a party.

items.en: refusing to change your mind or behaviour
items.example: He was too obstinate to admit that he had been wrong.

items.en: hopeful and positive about the future
items.example: Despite the delays, she remains sanguine about the project's chances.

items.en: saying very little and seeming unfriendly
items.example: Her taciturn father rarely said more than a few words at dinner.

items.en: generous and forgiving especially towards a rival
items.example: The winner was magnanimous and praised her opponent's skill.

items.en: (disapproving) too serious and proud of your own importance
items.example: The pompous speaker lectured us for an hour on his own achievements.

items.en: friendly and easy to talk to
items.example: The landlord was an affable man who always had time for a chat.

items.en: clever at understanding situations and using them well
items.example: An astute investor, Priya sold her shares before the crash.

items.en: changing mood quickly and often without warning
items.example: The director's mercurial temper made rehearsals tense.

items.en: talking a lot especially about unimportant things
items.example: The garrulous taxi driver talked all the way to the station.

items.en: paying great attention to detail and hard to please
